question: Some volunteers ate lunch in front of the television, others with no screen. What happened at the afternoon snack?
answer: The screen group ate more. A 2013 review of 24 studies found that distraction during a meal raised how much people ate at it, and raised what they ate later even more. A meal eaten half-noticed leaves a weak memory of having eaten, so the next craving meets little resistance.
move: Attention at a meal is part of what fills you.
ask: Do I eat my meals, or just get through them while doing something else?
trap: Both the same, since the screen did not change the lunch.
source: Robinson et al., Am. J. Clin. Nutr., 2013
reference: Robinson, Aveyard, Daley, Jolly, Lewis, Lycett & Higgs, Eating attentively: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of food intake memory and awareness on eating, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 2013
